claims.text: SWE-agent introduced the Agent-Computer Interface (ACI), a custom interface offering LM agents a small set of simple actions for viewing, searching and editing files, in contrast to the Linux shell's granular, highly configurable action space.
SWE-agent's ACI uses guardrails to prevent common mistakes, and the agent receives specific, concise feedback about a command's effects at every turn.

SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo solved 12.47% (286/2,294) of the full SWE-bench test set and 18.00% (54/300) of SWE-bench Lite, versus a previous best of 3.8% by a non-interactive retrieval-augmented system.
In the SWE-agent ablation on SWE-bench Lite, the ACI solved 10.7 percentage points more instances than a baseline agent using only the default Linux shell, a 64% relative increase with GPT-4 Turbo.
The SWE-agent ACI was developed for GPT-4 Turbo but ported to Claude 3 Opus, which solved 10.5% of SWE-bench tasks.
SWE-agent achieved pass@1 of 87.7% on HumanEvalFix (reported as 88.3% in a later table), and compared to RAG on SWE-bench Lite it was 8-13x more costly but yielded a 6.7-fold improved resolve rate.

In SWE-agent's GPT-4 Turbo full-split results, 266 of the resolved instances ended via an intentional submit command and 20 ended via cost-limit exit with submission, so most resolved tasks are intentionally submitted.
mini-SWE-agent, from the Princeton/Stanford SWE-agent team, uses roughly one hundred lines of Python for its core agent class and scores over 74% on SWE-bench Verified.

mini-SWE-agent uses bash as its sole tool, executed via standard subprocess calls so each action is independent and stateless, with the model using cat, sed/heredocs, grep/find and pytest rather than specialized commands.
mini-SWE-agent signals control flow with an exception hierarchy (InterruptAgentFlow: Submitted, LimitsExceeded, FormatError) whose messages are injected into history by run().
mini-SWE-agent has no context compaction and crashes with ContextWindowExceededError on overflow, keeps raw history unfiltered, and uses a single model throughout.
Mini-SWE-Agent implements all seven harness subsystems in roughly 100 lines, with a while loop, one template, one tool, a message list, and limits on steps, format errors and wall clock.

Spring-2026 self-reported SWE-Bench Verified figures were OpenHands 77.6%, Mini-SWE-Agent 74%+, Claude Code 72.7% and Codex 69.1%, using different models, and the study concludes loop sophistication does not predict benchmark performance.

OpenHands uses an event-sourced conversation loop over a persistent event log with parallel action batches governed by resource locks (default limit 1), and sandboxes via Docker, Apptainer or remote runtimes.
OpenHands uses an immutable EventStream with views computed from condensation markers, and compacts context via LLM summarization triggered at a token threshold.
OpenHands defaults to single-model operation through a noop router; its only implemented router (MultimodalRouter) decides based on image presence and token limits.

SWE-agent has 3 default tools (35 across 15 bundles), runs in Docker containers, and compacts context with 7 composable rule-based processors that keep the first and last N observations and elide the rest.

mini-SWE-agent is the only surveyed agent that edits files directly via shell commands rather than producing patches for the scaffold to apply, and provides process-level isolation without containerization.

OpenHands sandbox sessions run in a Docker container containing a bash shell, a Jupyter IPython server and a Playwright-controlled Chromium browser, with only task-relevant files exposed through workspace mounting.

OpenHands scored 60.6% on SWE-bench Verified at baseline and 66.4% with inference-time scaling (April 2025 blog post), while Docker isolation gives an ephemeral per-session environment that limits blast radius.
OpenHands with CodeAct v3 and Claude Opus 4.6 reached 68.4% on SWE-bench Verified, while Qwen3 Coder 480B reached 41.21%.

On SWE-bench-Live, OpenHands with Claude 3.7 scored 19.25% and SWE-Agent with GPT-4.1 scored 18.57%, with OpenHands re-running SWE-bench Verified at 43.20%, suggesting model choice matters more than framework on novel issues.

OpenHands-Versa, a generalist single agent built on OpenHands, gained 9.1 points on SWE-Bench Multimodal, 1.3 on GAIA and 9.1 on The Agent Company, and beat SWE-Agent variants by over 22 points on SWE-Bench M.

OpenHands supports MCP, multi-agent delegation, BrowserGym browser automation and enterprise RBAC/audit/quotas, whereas SWE-Agent is CLI-only with Docker/SWE-ReX sandboxing and an EnIGMA cybersecurity mode.
Goose was released by Block in January 2025 under Apache 2.0 and in 2026 moved to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation.
